clinicalPearls: Most severe cases follow ABO-incompatible transfusion, where recipient anti-A or anti-B antibodies bind donor red cells and trigger complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis
Classic features are fever, rigors, loin or back pain, a feeling of impending doom, hypotension, and haemoglobinuria appearing early during or soon after transfusion
The single most important action is to stop the transfusion immediately, maintain venous access, and provide supportive care with fluids to preserve renal perfusion
Disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute kidney injury are the feared complications and drive much of the mortality
Most fatal reactions arise from clerical error and misidentification of the patient or sample rather than from any failure of the laboratory crossmatch
Send the implicated unit and fresh patient samples back to the laboratory for a clerical recheck, repeat group and crossmatch, and direct antiglobulin test
In an anaesthetised or unconscious patient, unexplained hypotension, bleeding from wound sites, and haemoglobinuria may be the only clues
reference.pathophysiology: An acute haemolytic transfusion reaction occurs when preformed recipient antibodies bind antigens on transfused donor red cells. In ABO incompatibility, naturally occurring IgM anti-A or anti-B fixes complement efficiently, driving rapid intravascular haemolysis with release of free haemoglobin and red-cell stroma. Complement activation and the resulting cytokine surge produce fever, vasodilatation and hypotension, while procoagulant material triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation. Free haemoglobin and reduced renal perfusion combine to cause acute tubular injury and kidney failure. The severity broadly tracks the volume of incompatible cells infused and the complement-fixing capacity of the antibody involved.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial contamination of the transfused unit with septic reaction
Non-immune haemolysis from mechanical or thermal red-cell damage
additionalInvestigations: Immediate clerical recheck of patient identity, unit label and compatibility documentation
Direct antiglobulin test on a post-transfusion sample and repeat ABO grouping and crossmatch on donor and recipient
Markers of haemolysis including lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin and a blood film
Free plasma and urinary haemoglobin to confirm intravascular haemolysis
Coagulation screen, fibrinogen and platelet count to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation
Renal function and urine output monitoring for acute kidney injury
redFlags: Hypotension, rigors and loin pain developing within minutes of starting a transfusion
Haemoglobinuria with oliguria signalling evolving acute kidney injury
Oozing from cannula and wound sites suggesting disseminated intravascular coagulation
Cardiovascular collapse in an anaesthetised patient with unexplained haemoglobinuria
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the volume of incompatible blood infused and the speed of recognition; prompt cessation and supportive care are often survivable, but large-volume ABO-incompatible transfusions carry a high risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury and death.
pitfalls: Attributing early fever to a benign febrile reaction and continuing the transfusion
Failing to perform a clerical recheck, which most often reveals the underlying identification error
Overlooking haemoglobinuria and evolving renal impairment in a sedated or ventilated patient
Delaying supportive fluid resuscitation while awaiting laboratory confirmation
